# Introduction

`CATEomics` estimates conditional average treatment effects (CATE) for
high-dimensional omics data (many genes, few samples). Many CATE estimators
exist and no single one is reliably best in advance: the winner depends on the
data. `CATEomics` therefore provides one interface to **compare** estimators on
proxy losses, **select** one, or **combine** them into an ensemble, and to
carry the resulting individual effects into standard Bioconductor analyses.

This vignette walks through that workflow on a small simulated
`SummarizedExperiment`. The data are synthetic and used only to make the steps
runnable end to end.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("matsui-lab/CATEomics")
```

```{r libs, message = FALSE}
library(CATEomics)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
```

The Python-backed estimators (the meta-learners and the neural methods) run
in a Python environment that `basilisk` [@lun2022] provisions on first use, which takes
a few minutes the first time and nothing afterwards. The R packages the default
estimators and the scoring need are hard dependencies. A few features read
packages from `Suggests` --- the `bcf` method, batch correction, gene-set
scoring and the SHAP plots --- and so do the downstream recipes at the end.

# Example data

`cf_example_data()` returns a `SummarizedExperiment` of raw RNA-seq counts with
a randomised treatment, a continuous outcome, two clinical covariates
(`age`, `sex`) and a planted heterogeneous treatment effect. The true
individual effect is stored in `colData` and the signal genes are flagged in
`rowData`. The gene names are drawn from the MSigDB hallmark collection
[@liberzon2015].

The default `ate = 0` puts the average effect at zero, so about half the
samples are harmed by treatment and which patients benefit --- not the average
--- is the interesting quantity here. Every constant of the generating process
is an argument (`effect_size`, `ate`, `noise_sd`, and the number of signal
genes), and `?cf_example_data` gives the formulas.

```{r data}
se <- cf_example_data(n = 150, p = 600, seed = 1)
se
colData(se)[1:3, ]
```

# A single estimator

`cf_fit()` fits one method. The ten methods and where each one is computed:

| `method` | estimator comes from | needs Python |
|---|---|---|
| `grf` | `grf` | no |
| `bcf` | `bcf` | no |
| `slearner` | CATEomics itself | yes |
| `tlearner` | `econml` | yes |
| `xlearner` | `econml` | yes |
| `drlearner` | `econml` | yes |
| `cevae` | `pyro` | yes |
| `ganite` | CATEomics itself | yes |
| `tarnet` | `catenets` | yes |
| `dragonnet` | `catenets` | yes |

The two CATEomics implementations are written with `scikit-learn` and `torch`
respectively. Each method has its own help page, which carries the reference for the
estimator it implements and the hyperparameters it accepts (`?cf_fit_grf`,
`?cf_fit_xlearner`, and so on).

Only the four meta / DR learners (`slearner`, `tlearner`, `xlearner`,
`drlearner`) take a pluggable base learner for the outcome; `grf` and the
neural methods estimate their own nuisance functions internally, and `bcf`
fits the outcome with its own BART but takes a learner for the propensity
(`model_propensity`, default `logistic`). The seven base
learners are `linear` / `logistic`, `lasso` / `ridge` / `elastic_net`, `rf`
and `xgboost`. `model_outcome` picks the outcome model and `model_final` the
second-stage CATE model. Only `xlearner` and `drlearner` take `model_final`:
`xlearner` falls back to `model_outcome` when it is not given, `drlearner`
does not and uses `ridge`.

The example below uses `grf` [@athey2019], which is R-native and needs no
Python. The result carries the average effect and one estimate per sample.

CATEomics treats **larger values of `Y` as the better outcome**, so a positive
`tau_hat` is a treatment that helps and the functions downstream -- benefit
groups, the treatment rule, the evaluation metrics and the plots -- all read
the largest `tau_hat` as the most benefit. If smaller values of your outcome
are better, such as a severity score, analyse the negated outcome (`-Y`, or
`1 - Y` for a binary one).

`X_baseline` names the clinical covariates in `colData`; the omics block comes
from the assay. `omics = "all"`, the default for a `SummarizedExperiment`,
takes the whole assay; a character vector names features instead, and
`"none"` leaves the omics out. When a `SummarizedExperiment` has several
assays, name the one to use: assays are not combined. A
`MultiAssayExperiment` takes every experiment `omics` points at, concatenates
them and prefixes each column with its experiment's name (`rnaseq_GENE1`); a
named list such as `list(rnaseq = "all", methyl = c("cg001"))` selects per
experiment. `?cf_fit` has the full grammar, including what a `data.frame`
accepts.

What reaches the design matrix is then filtered. `feature_method` defaults to
`"variance"`, which keeps the most variable columns; the alternatives are
`"none"` (no filtering), `"pca"` (principal components) and `"pathway"`
(gene-set scores). `n_features` defaults to 100 (50 per layer for a
`MultiAssayExperiment`) and sets how many columns, components or gene sets are
kept. The calls below pass `n_features = 300`.

```{r grf}
fit <- cf_fit(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
              X_baseline = c("age", "sex"), omics = "all",
              method = "grf", n_features = 300)
fit
head(predict(fit, type = "tau"))
```

# Comparing estimators

To put several estimators on the same footing, fit them with `cf_compare()`.
It uses one K-fold split for all of them --- each method fits on K-1 folds and
predicts the fold it did not see --- and scores those out-of-fold estimates on
proxy CATE losses, where a lower loss is better.

`metric` says which losses to compute and defaults to all three: `r_loss`
[@nie2021], `dr_loss` [@kennedy2023; @mahajan2024] and `factual_loss`. The
`rank` column is taken on the first of them, so to rank on another loss, put
that one first. To leave the scoreboard as it is and choose on a different
loss, name it in `cf_select()` instead.

The losses are computed from nuisance models fitted separately from the
candidates. Since the preprocessing, the split and those nuisance models are
the same for every candidate, differences in loss reflect differences in the
candidates' estimates. The nuisance models come from a Super Learner by
default (`eval_nuisance = "super_learner"` [@vanderlaan2007]).

The propensity is estimated by default, from the clinical covariates. To
estimate it from particular variables only, name them in `propensity_X`. When
the assignment probability is known by design, pass it instead:
`propensity_score` gives it to the estimators and `eval_propensity_score` to
the scoring. This is a randomised trial, so both are `0.5`.

```{r compare}
methods <- c("grf", "tlearner", "xlearner")
cmp <- cf_compare(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
                  X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
                  methods = methods,
                  n_features = 300, model_outcome = "lasso",
                  propensity_score = 0.5, eval_propensity_score = 0.5,
                  random_state = 1)
cmp
```

`model_outcome` and `propensity_score` are offered to every candidate, and
not every method takes them: `grf` estimates its outcome inside its own
forest, and `tlearner` uses no propensity score. A candidate a setting did
not reach is named, so a value that went nowhere is not read as part of the
fit.

The `between_fold_share` column is the share of the variance of the
out-of-fold effects that the fold assignment explains. Near 0 the spread is
between individuals; near 1 the method returned close to one value per fold,
and its ranking of individuals carries little. By default it prints only the
loss the rank was taken on; `print(cmp, full = TRUE)` also shows the other two
losses, their intervals and the squared scores.

The scoreboard answers one question --- which of these methods --- and looking
at it raises the next ones.

## Trying several base learners

A meta learner [@kunzel2019b] or a DR learner [@kennedy2023] fits its outcome
model with the learner `model_outcome` names. The second-stage CATE model is `model_final`, and when that is not
given, `xlearner` follows `model_outcome` while `drlearner` does not and uses
`ridge`.

The comparison above named one learner and ran it. **To try several instead,
pass `base_learners`**: each meta / DR learner comes back as one row per base
learner, named `xlearner_rf` and so on. Under `base_learners` the outcome
model and the final model are always the same estimator. `grf`, `bcf` and the
neural methods build their own nuisance models, so there is nothing to swap
and they stay on one row.

```{r compare-base, eval = FALSE}
cmp_grid <- cf_compare(data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment",
                       X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
                       methods = c("grf", "xlearner"),
                       base_learners = c("lasso", "rf"),
                       n_features = 300,
                       propensity_score = 0.5, eval_propensity_score = 0.5,
                       random_state = 1)
```

## Setting the hyperparameters

**Where you write a block in `params` decides what it reaches.** Written under
a candidate's label (`xlearner_rf`) it reaches that candidate; written under a
method name (`xlearner`) it reaches every candidate made from that method.
When a candidate has both, only the label's block is used: the two are not
merged.

A method's own hyperparameters go in flat (`grf = list(num.trees = )`), and a
base learner's go in the slot that learner fills (`outcome` and `final`). A
name the method does not take is an error rather than a quiet default, and
anything that has to be a whole number is written `10L`, since the Python
libraries check the type. The last line of the print names what each candidate
resolved to, so the losses and the settings are read off the same screen; a
long line is cut, and `cmp$metadata$params` holds all of it.

```{r compare-params}
cmp_tuned <- cf_compare(
  data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment", X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
  methods = c("grf", "xlearner"), base_learners = c("lasso", "rf"),
  n_features = 300, propensity_score = 0.5, eval_propensity_score = 0.5,
  random_state = 1,
  params = list(
    grf            = list(num.trees = 4000),
    xlearner_lasso = list(outcome = list(cv = 10L),
                          final   = list(cv = 10L)),
    xlearner_rf    = list(outcome = list(n_estimators = 300L, max_depth = 4L),
                          final   = list(n_estimators = 300L, max_depth = 4L))))
cmp_tuned
```

## Comparing candidates you configure yourself

Sometimes the comparison is not between methods but between settings --- one
causal forest grown shallow against the same forest grown deep --- or between
slots: the same outcome model with a different second stage. **`params` only
configures candidates; it cannot add any**, and the candidates `base_learners`
makes have the same estimator in both slots. `configs` is the form that sets
each candidate on its own.

**`configs` writes the candidates out and lets you name them.** Those names
are what the scoreboard, `cf_select()`, `cf_ensemble()` and the plots call
them from then on. The settings are written per candidate, so there is no key
deciding what a block reaches: a candidate's `params` is its own method's
block.

```{r compare-configs}
cmp_cfg <- cf_compare(
  data = se, Y = "outcome", T = "treatment", X_baseline = c("age", "sex"),
  n_features = 300, propensity_score = 0.5, eval_propensity_score = 0.5,
  random_state = 1,
  configs = list(
    grf_shallow    = list(method = "grf",
                          params = list(num.trees = 500,  min.node.size = 15)),
    grf_deep       = list(method = "grf",
                          params = list(num.trees = 4000, min.node.size = 1)),
    xlearner_lasso = list(method = "xlearner", model_outcome = "lasso",
                          model_final = "lasso"),
    xlearner_ridge = list(method = "xlearner", model_outcome = "lasso",
                          model_final = "ridge")))
cmp_cfg
```

The first two rows are the same method under different settings; the last two
share an outcome model and differ only in the second stage.


# How much do methods agree?

`cf_model_stability()` reports how much the methods order the patients the
same way: the correlation between every pair of per-patient estimates, the
range those pairwise values span, and each method's mean correlation with the
rest. A high value says the methods agree, not that any of them is right.

```{r stability}
cf_model_stability(cmp)
```

# Selecting or combining

`cf_select()` returns the method with the lowest loss on the scoreboard
`cf_compare()` produced. `cf_ensemble()` instead combines the per-patient
effects across methods, with one of five weighting rules: `mean` (equal
weights), `softmax` (weights decreasing in the loss), `r_stacking` and
`dr_stacking` (weights that minimise the R-loss or the DR-loss
[@nie2021; @hanwu2022]) and `cba` (a correlation-based choice of a sub-group
of methods, averaged with equal weights). `r_stacking`, used here, solves
non-negative weights and can leave a method at zero.

```{r select-ensemble}
sel <- cf_select(cmp)
sel$selection_stats$selected_method

ens <- cf_ensemble(cmp, method = "r_stacking")
ens
```

# Evaluating a chosen model

Individual effects are never observed, but a per-patient pseudo-outcome that
equals the true CATE on average can be built from the observed outcomes, and
`cf_evaluate()` scores the estimates against it. The rank-weighted average
treatment effect family (RATE: the targeting operator characteristic TOC at a
given treated fraction and its average AUTOC; @yadlowsky2025) and the sorted
group average treatment effects (GATES; @chernozhukov2025) average the
pseudo-outcome within groups of patients ranked by the estimates, and so test
whether patients with larger estimates really have larger effects. The best
linear predictor (BLP; @chernozhukov2025) regresses the pseudo-outcome on the
estimates: a slope of 1 says the estimates are on the right scale, a slope of
0 says there is no relationship to detect. `cf_evaluate()` reuses the
evaluation nuisance the comparison already fitted, so the score stays the one
the scoreboard was built on.

```{r evaluate}
winner <- cmp$models[[sel$selection_stats$selected_method]]
ev <- cf_evaluate(winner)
ev
```

`cf_plot_evaluate()` draws any of the three: the TOC curve, the sorted group
effects, or the BLP calibration.

```{r plot-rate, fig.cap = "TOC curve of the selected model."}
cf_plot_evaluate(ev, type = "rate")
```

# Which genes drive the effect?

`cf_interpret()` distils a fitted model (or the ensemble) into a surrogate
SHAP explanation [@lundberg2017]: an importance and a direction per gene. Two
surrogates are fitted, a ridge regression and a gradient-boosted tree
(`"ridge"` and `"xgb"`), and each reports a `fidelity`: the held-out $R^2$
of that surrogate on the estimated effect. We use the ensemble effect here.

```{r interpret}
itp <- cf_interpret(ens)
# `vi` is keyed by surrogate; each holds a per-gene importance/direction table.
itp$vi$ridge$fidelity
head(itp$vi$ridge$features)
```

# Benefit groups and a treatment rule

`cf_benefit_groups()` splits patients into high- and low-benefit groups from
the (out-of-fold) estimated effects.

```{r groups}
grp <- cf_benefit_groups(ens)
grp
```

`cf_rule()` turns the estimates into a treat / do-not-treat rule and estimates
its **policy value**: the mean outcome that would be observed if patients were
treated according to the rule [@athey2021]. On its own that number is hard to
read, so it is reported against three fixed policies --- treating everyone,
treating no one, and treating the same number of patients at random. The
comparison with the random policy of the same budget is the one that isolates
what the rule built from the estimates adds: it holds the number treated fixed
and changes only who is chosen.

```{r rule}
rule <- cf_rule(ens, type = "threshold", threshold = 0, random_state = 1)
rule
```

Sweeping the threshold with `grid = TRUE` gives the policy value as a function
of the treated fraction, which `cf_plot_policy_curve()` draws against the
same-budget random baseline.

```{r plot-policy, fig.cap = "Policy value against the treated fraction, with the same-budget random baseline (dashed)."}
rule_grid <- cf_rule(ens, type = "threshold", grid = TRUE, random_state = 1)
cf_plot_policy_curve(rule_grid)
```

# Connecting to Bioconductor: a biology-bridge recipe

The workflow's output lives naturally on the `SummarizedExperiment`. Write the
estimated effect and benefit group back with `cf_attach_results()`, then use
standard Bioconductor tools [@huber2015] to describe the biology of the
benefit groups.

```{r attach}
se <- cf_attach_results(se, ens, what = c("tau", "group"), groups = grp)
colData(se)[1:3, c("cf_tau", "cf_group")]
```

**Differential expression between benefit groups** with `limma` [@ritchie2015],
its `voom` weights [@law2014] and `edgeR` [@chen2025; @robinson2010]:

```{r deg, eval = requireNamespace("limma", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("edgeR", quietly = TRUE)}
library(edgeR); library(limma)
grp_f  <- factor(colData(se)$cf_group)
dge    <- DGEList(assay(se, "counts"))
dge    <- dge[filterByExpr(dge, group = grp_f), , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dge    <- normLibSizes(dge)
design <- model.matrix(~ grp_f)
efit   <- eBayes(lmFit(voom(dge, design), design))
topTable(efit, coef = 2, number = 5)[, c("logFC", "adj.P.Val")]
```

**Pathway activity related to the estimated benefit**: `GSVA`
[@hanzelmann2013] scores each hallmark gene set per sample with ssGSEA
[@barbie2009], and the recipe then examines the correlation between those
scores and the individual effect (`cf_tau`):

```{r gsva, eval = requireNamespace("GSVA", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("msigdbr", quietly = TRUE)}
library(GSVA); library(msigdbr)
h    <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
sets <- split(h$gene_symbol, h$gs_name)
logcpm <- edgeR::cpm(assay(se, "counts"), log = TRUE)
scores <- gsva(ssgseaParam(logcpm, sets), verbose = FALSE)
tau    <- colData(se)$cf_tau
cors   <- sort(apply(scores, 1, cor, tau, method = "spearman"), decreasing = TRUE)
head(cors, 3)
```

These descriptions are exploratory: the groups and scores derive from the
estimated effect, so treat the associations as hypothesis-generating.

# The rest of the API

The functions above are the path through the workflow. Two more analysis
functions and the remaining plots are not used here:

| function | what it does |
|---|---|
| `cf_aggregate_vi()` | Runs `cf_interpret()` on every candidate in a comparison and merges their per-gene importance rankings into one consensus list by robust rank aggregation. |
| `cf_diagnostics()` | Reports the assumptions behind the estimates: the propensity distribution and how many values the clipping moved, the standardised mean differences after preprocessing, the covariate distributions by arm, and the E-value for unmeasured confounding. |

| plot | what it draws |
|---|---|
| `cf_plot_compare()` | The scoreboard as ranked bars for one loss. |
| `cf_plot_stability()` | The pairwise correlation matrix from `cf_model_stability()`. |
| `cf_plot_cate()` | The distribution of the per-patient effects of one fit, with the average effect marked. |
| `cf_plot_interpret()` | The SHAP output of `cf_interpret()`: importance bars, a beeswarm, or the dependence on one gene. |
| `cf_plot_rule()` | The policy tree of `cf_rule(type = "tree")`, with each leaf labelled by what it does. |
| `cf_plot_diagnostics()` | Three views of `cf_diagnostics()`: the propensity overlap, the standardised mean differences, and one covariate by arm. |
